## Verdicts

Verdicts 56 to 114 are settled, said under each in REVIEW-ARCHIVE.md; Verdict 115 is open on the

115. **The pack run of `894542da` is red in its games job, e3d finding no session for a game that
    serves, its session's file written after the look.** In the pack run with publish 42985743208,
    started at 09:16 on 2026-11-11, the games job failed after 85 minutes at the step that resizes
    each game while it draws, Manor's storm ending with NO_SESSION two seconds after Manor served as
    pid 32988; every game before it and after it passed its storm, and the suites, the captures on
    Linux and macOS and the examples are green, the first Windows half going. The error's account,
    added at `8da28e48` for Verdict 113, names the cause that verdict could only infer. The sessions
    folder holds 32988.json, pid 32988, Manor, its heartbeat 5.0 s old, which runs and matches,
    written after the look. So the client looked while the served program was writing its session's
    file again and found none to take, a race between the heartbeat's write and the client's read,
    and Siege's stop in Verdict 113 reads as the same race. The mend is on both sides, the served
    program writing its session's file whole beside the old one and renaming it over, so a reader
    finds the old or the new and never neither, and the client looking again for a short while
    before it says no session where the folder holds a file of a running program; with a test that a
    client looking while a program writes its heartbeat many times over never reports no session.
    After the tail's commit in work, before any further cut of 250. The failed job is run again when
    the run ends, the fault being one of timing, so the package for the game comes of this commit.
    Written at 12:07 on 2026-11-11. Corrected at 12:27 by the coder's read. The served program
    already writes its session's file whole and renames it over, the heartbeat was 5.0 s old and so
    not being written at the look, and written after the look is the label the account gives any
    matching file found after a look that failed, so the review read a label as a cause and the race
    it named is not shown; 20,000 looks against 28,659 rewrites here found no miss. What is seen is
    that a look naming no session looks once where a named one looks five times over a second. The
    datum left is the heartbeat's age, 5.0 s in a game two seconds into serving at the start of a
    storm on lavapipe; so before the mend, what a look asks of a heartbeat's age and how often and
    from which thread the heartbeat is written, since a frame of several seconds would leave it old
    and a look asking a fresh one would find no session while the program runs, as Siege was found.
    The mend follows that read, the session live by its process with the age said and not asked or
    the heartbeat written off the frame's thread, or else the looks made five with the cause unseen
    and the label made true. The two reads by 12:27. A look asks nothing of a heartbeat's age, a
    session being live where its process runs, and a lone session past the 5 s of patience is still
    chosen; the heartbeat is written every 30 frames by the frame's thread, which explains the 5.0 s
    at the start of a storm on lavapipe and nothing else. So the cause stays unseen. The mend,
    approved, the unnamed look made as the named one, five looks over a second, with its test and
    the account's label made true; and with it each look keeps what it itself saw, the error
    carrying the first failed look's own record, each file whether read, parsed and its process
    found, with any exception's text, and a read or a process's check that throws is said and not
    turned into a file passed over, so a next time names itself.

94. **No millisecond budget.** The owner wrote on 2026-11-08 at 08:50, "There is no ms limit budget.
   We first make it work and performant and focus on crunching the numbers after or along the way as
   much as possible." So the GI budgets of Decision 84 and item 208's 4 ms at High are no gate, and
   a mend that brings a view to its reference lands by its figures, its cost measured and recorded
   beside them and cut after or along the way where a cut holds the readings, the quality levels
   keeping their names and not their milliseconds. Item 208 closes; the parked forms of items 213
   and 212 are read again by their figures alone, item 217.

95. **A stop rule, one target and one lever.** The owner wrote on 2026-11-08 at 08:5x, asked why the
   light leaking had moved little in days, that the review should do what it thinks right and tell
   them for approval. The owner approved at 08:49 on 2026-11-08 ("Do it"), so three things hold for
   the GI work. A view inside its band lands and a figure that remains is recorded and not chased,
   unless it lies in a scene the owner looks at, Sponza's named views here and the meadow in the
   bridge; one bounded read places a cause, and a second is the last before a mend is tried or the
   figure recorded. The vestibule's door at 8:00 is the engine's one target scene until it is in its
   band, the rest of Sponza within its bands already. And one structural lever is read before more
   patches, the probes' texels at 16 by 16 in the near cascades, since the carried probes' sliver,
   the corridor's over-read, the side wall's echo and the door's pocket parts all trace to an 8 by 8
   texel, item 218.

96. **The owner's flicker recordings.** The owner put two F2 recordings and three screenshots of
   scenes_sponza's balcony view in the dump of 2026-11-08 at 11:08 to 11:09 and wrote that it
   flickers still, a basic flicker through the first 76 pictures, the hour switched forth and back
   from 77 to 85, and then a flicker right after movement or a light recalculation that settles
   after a time, more visible at steep angles and thin surfaces. Measured here picture to picture,
   the idle 76 pictures move 1.3% of the pixels by 12 levels or more at some time and 0.36 by 25,
   along the right wall's steep edge, the arches' edges and undersides, the columns and the far
   windows; after the hour's change 6.4 and 1.4% move over the next 24 pictures, settling in about a
   second and a half; the second recording's largest step moves 0.6% at the same places. So the
   flicker the owner sees is small in pixels and lies where the readings of 205 and 210 did not
   look, the steep-angle edges a held view's whole-frame figure averages out. Item 219, first in the
   order since it is in the scene the owner looks at.

    too, and answered the review's questions at 14:1x. The form is `v6.0.91`, the letter v before
    `build/version.sh`'s number. Tags go on each major or minor change and on the commits packages
    were built from, since "doing every commit clutters it and is unnecessary as we want to focus
    the version tags to releases time apart with meaningful changes and not commits apart". The
    major and the minor are the sessions' to raise, "each session working on the project can decide
    when the time is right to rise that number in minor or major as each commit counts as patch",
    with "full liberty" when "a step is done and meaningful changes were done". N 6.3 holds the rule
    and the reviewer sets the tags as it pushes. `v6.0.0` marks the commit that set 6.0 and
    `v6.0.91` the commit `f14a9530` the package of 6.0.91 was published from on 2026-11-04, both set
    at 14:2x.

101. **No middle dot.** The owner wrote at 17:57 and 18:00 on 2026-11-08 that the middle dot is not
    used, the README's top links separated by a space alone and the dot nowhere else; the reviewer
    changed the README's first line in the tree on their word, for the next commit to carry, and
    every other middle dot in the repository is item 224's. The rule goes into STYLE.md's
    Punctuation as the shared text has it everywhere.

102. **One repository, many projects.** The owner wrote at about 18:20 on 2026-11-08, thinking with
    the review about the engines' future after Unity Essentials, where every feature is a repository
    of its own, that the engines feel "a bit cluttered" and should be "modulated extendable and
    stable and easy to use", that splitting everything into repositories "clutters" and makes
    commits "weird", that the shared modules' repositories are right, that the engine's own content
    could be modulated the same way inside its repository, and that a "one process approach", one
    running process edited and seen as it changes, is worth thinking about; at 18:30 they approved
    the review's recommendation. The direction is that each engine stays one repository and becomes
    one solution of many projects, each an area with its own public surface and its own plugin,
    packed as its own package at one version for all, as Bevy's crates are in Bevy's one repository;
    the dependency direction is held by project references and a norm test over them; the flat API
    stays unchanged on top and a game names the packages it needs; the names are dotted .NET names
    and not com.; there is no editor, and the live path is a watcher that recompiles a changed
    shader, reloads a changed asset or scene and recompiles a changed behavior into the running
    process, the engine's own code by restart. It is scheduled after the current items and done as
    one mechanical batch per engine with the public API held identical before and after and the
    documents' tables redrawn. Items 225 and 226, BevyCSharp Decision 85.

103. **Comments on the code's own terms.** The owner read a comment of scenes_sponza at about 19:00
    on 2026-11-08, "The frame graded as that scene's HDRP profile grades it, by the look of its AgX
    - Powerful.exr, a lookup build/unity-lut.py writes from that strip, a gamma of w 0.225, and a
    bloom of intensity 0.25, threshold 0.333 and scatter 0.7, worked out as HDRP works them out",
    and wrote that it "sounds just bad", reads as an em dash, and "is taking too much liberty of
    outside knowledge and in-process session knowledge", in scenes_sponza explicitly and probably
    everywhere else. The rule from it, in STYLE.md's Register and as N 4.11, is that a comment
    stands on the code's own terms. It says what the code does and why in the engine's words; a
    number taken from elsewhere stands with the reason it is right here, what it makes the frame or
    the program do, and the source is named once in the documents' references and not in the
    comment; the file names of outside assets, another product's profile or process as the
    explanation, "as X works it out", and the facts of the sessions' work are not written in a
    comment. Item 227, BevyCSharp Decision 86.

108. **Post-processing settings in plain numbers.** The owner asked at 21:59 on 2026-11-09, reading

Item 253, the lock. Since 8da28e48 every pipeline made through the driver's cache waited for the
one lock, so a compile on the frame's thread and a mirror's on a worker ran one after the other.
A trial with a mirror plane, a shader of the program's own drawn in the mirror and the window from
the frame the plane is set, and every pipeline held a second in the driver by the test's hook: on
the head the two compiles on workers and the window's on the frame's thread began at 11, 1,011 and
2,030 ms and the first frame took 3,040 ms; with the compiles sharing the lock they began within
38 ms and the frame took 1,057 ms. As the specification reads, a cache made without
VK_PIPELINE_CACHE_CREATE_EXTERNALLY_SYNCHRONIZED_BIT asks no external synchronization of
vkCreateGraphicsPipelines, vkCreateComputePipelines or vkGetPipelineCacheData, and asks it of
vkMergePipelineCaches' destination and of vkDestroyPipelineCache. So the compiles now share the
lock, and the read of the cache's data for the write and the cache's release hold it alone. The
write held alone beside the compiles is kept because it is cheap, as Verdict 113 asked, and was
never shown needed, since that stop was never seen again. A test holds one compile in the driver
and finds another thread's finished beside it, which on the single lock waited past 15 s;
8da28e48's test that the write waits for a compile in flight passes as it did.

Verdict 115, read. The served program writes its session's file whole as {pid}.json.tmp and moves
it over the old with File.Move and overwrite, a rename on Linux, so a reader finds the old or the
new and never neither; a trial here rewrote one 28,659 times while 20,000 looks that named no
session listed the folder, and none found no session. The heartbeat is written every 30 frames by
the served program's Stage.First on the frame's thread, so a frame of seconds in a storm on
lavapipe leaves it as old, which Manor's 5.0 s is; but no look asks its age: Running is the
process alive and nothing more, and a lone stale session is still chosen, so the age explains the
5.0 s and not the miss. What did differ is that a storm names no session, and an unnamed look was
made once where a named one is made five times a fifth of a second apart. The cause on the runner
stays unseen. The client's look now goes through CliSessionFile.Serving, every serving app or
those asked for, looked for again as a named one is. Each look keeps what it saw of each file, read
or not with the words of the exception where its read threw, its pid and whether its process runs
or why not, where asking it threw with its words, and the error carries the first failed look's
record before the folder read again after the looks, whose label now says it was found then, where
it said written after the look, which it does not know. Read and Running caught their exceptions
and turned them into a file passed over and a process taken as gone, unsaid; the record says them.
The tests find a session written after an unnamed first look at the second, which a single look
does not, and a look's record saying a read that threw with its words.
